The underground powerhouse chamber would be about 75 feet wide, 147 feet high, and 438 feet long. It would contain 4 reversible, single stage, Francis type pump-turbines, each direct-connected to a 3-phase, vertical shaft, 60-cycle, generator-motor, rated at 250,000 kilowatts generating and 345,000 horsepower as a motor with a maximum temperature rise of 60oC. Each unit would be controlled by a turbine governor and each would be equipped with direct-connected starting motors capable of accelerating the pumps to synchronous speed. Total capacity of the 4 units would be 1,000,000 kW when operated as generators and 1,380,000 hp when operated as motors.
Two 400-ton traveling bridge cranes would be mounted on rails above the powerhouse operating floor for erecting, dismantling, and servicing the pumping-generating units.
Four concrete-lined draft tube tunnels, each about 280 feet long and 14.5 feet in diameter, would connect by means of a manifold structure to two concrete-lined tailrace tunnels, each approximately 900 feet long and 26.5 feet in diameter. The tailrace tunnel would terminate at an outlet structure with invert at elevation 1,050 feet on Lake Jocassee.
The reinforced concrete outlet structure would be equipped with five 15-foot-wide and 25-foot-high steel lift gates, each controlled by a 40-ton fixed hoist.
Lake Jocassee is the upper pool of the Jocassee Pumped Storage Development under FPC license as project No. 2503 and would serve as the lower pool of the Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project. The lower 6 feet of usable storage in Lake Jocassee (between elevation 1,080 and 1,086 feet), representing 41,000 acre-feet of water, was specifically reserved for the operation of future pumped storage projects and was fully contemplated at the time of licensing the Keowee-Toxaway Project. The Bad Creek Project would draw from this reserve.
At full pool elevation 1,110 feet, Lake Jocassee has a water surface area of 7,565 acres and a storage storage capacity of 1,160,300 acre-feet. At full pool the Jocassee Reservoir water surface would be about 35 feet above the top of the Bad Creek Powerhouse discharge
